The assignments as Klass prints them: entered the Army 8 July 1968; after basic training 'he was trained to be a clerk/typist'; Vietnam February 1970 to August 1972 'where his duties are listed as clerk/typist'; Fort Gordon and Fort Knox, principal duty clerk/typist; 'as of March 1975 his duty is shown as administration specialist'; August 1976 to August 1983 in Germany as administration specialist; then Keesler AFB and Fort Gordon as 'Det. claims.text: AFFIRMATIVE EVIDENCE AGAINST THE ACCOUNT, NOT MERELY AN ABSENCE. Klass records: 'Stone claims that he and his Army team were sent to the USAF Bentwaters base in England in late December of 1980 to investigate a UFO incident... A further challenge to this claim is that on Dec. 23, 1983, Stone made a Freedom Of Information Act (FOIA) request to the USAF for information on the Bentwaters UFO incident which he would have acquired during his (alleged) official visit in 1980. Further, Stone's request used his home address and did not show that he was an Army sergeant.' This is an act by Stone, three years after the event, inconsistent with his own later account of having been there officially.

claims.text: STATED INFERENCE. Klass and Randle are not two agents sharing a method. One worked from a records request to the National Personnel Records Center; the other from thirty years of personal acquaintance and is a retired Air Force officer who argues for the reality of other cases. The corollary in CLAUDE.md section 2 about two agents agreeing under a shared method does not apply to this pair.

conflicts: His own testimony places him in NBC duties and in the 96th Civil Affairs Company. The assignment list Klass prints from the National Personnel Records Center record contains no NBC billet and no Civil Affairs unit; it runs clerk/typist, administration specialist, detachment sergeant, chief administrative clerk. The two descriptions of the same career are not compatible and the board carries both rather than resolving them, because the NPRC record itself was not opened here.

He told the Disclosure Project that his team was sent to Bentwaters in late December 1980. Klass notes that the incident was not reported to higher officials until roughly two weeks after Stone says his team arrived.

label: Clifford E. Stone
narrative: Clifford Stone is on this board because the evidence against his extraordinary account is unusually good, not because the account is. His ordinary career is a federal record and it was obtained: Philip J. Klass requested it from the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis and printed the assignments in the summer of 2001, and they run clerk/typist from basic training, clerk/typist in Vietnam from February 1970 to August 1972, administration specialist from March 1975, seven years in Germany, detachment sergeant, and from May 1985 chief administrative clerk at the New Mexico Military Institute. Kevin Randle, who is already a node on this board, who met Stone in February 1989 and visited his home many times, independently records the same shape: four claimed Vietnam tours against a record showing thirty-seven months overseas and not all of it in Vietnam, and nothing in the record supporting the story of slipping out at night to hunt the enemy. Those are two genuinely independent methods, a records request and a thirty-year acquaintance, and one of the two men spent his career arguing that other UFO cases are real. But the item that matters most is not an absence at all. It is something Stone did. He told the Disclosure Project that an Army team took him to Bentwaters in England in late December 1980 to investigate the incident there. On 23 December 1983, three years later, he filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the United States Air Force asking for information about that same incident, from his home address, without indicating that he was a serving Army sergeant. A man who had been there officially does not write in as a member of the public for the file. The record also contains something in his favour and it belongs here: after he was relieved for administrative inefficiency in January 1988, an Army investigation cleared him and he was later awarded the Meritorious Service Medal for the work he had been criticised over.

timeline.label: Clifford Stone enters the US Army
timeline.text: Per the service record Philip J. Klass obtained from the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis and printed in 2001: Stone entered the Army on 8 July 1968 and after several months of basic training 'he was trained to be a clerk/typist'. The assignment history that follows is clerical and administrative throughout.

timeline.label: Stone files a FOIA request about Bentwaters, from his home address
timeline.text: Klass records that on 23 December 1983 Clifford Stone filed a Freedom of Information Act request with the USAF for information on the Bentwaters incident, 'used his home address and did not show that he was an Army sergeant'. Stone had told the Disclosure Project that an Army team took him there officially in late December 1980. THIS IS AN AFFIRMATIVE ACT INCONSISTENT WITH HIS OWN ACCOUNT, NOT AN ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE.

timeline.label: Clifford Stone's testimony recorded for the Disclosure Project
timeline.text: Printed at section 3.8.4 under 'Testimony of Sergeant Clifford Stone, United States Army / September 2000'. The editorial header: 'Stone has seen living and dead extraterrestrials in his official duties on an army team that retrieved crashed ET crafts.'

timeline.label: Clifford Stone dies at Roswell
timeline.text: Kevin Randle: 'Clifford E. Stone, known for his relentless pursuit of UFO documentation through his use of FOIA died on February 10, in Roswell, New Mexico.' Randle sets out in the same post the discrepancies between Stone's account and his service record.
